digest.definition: Computing studies how computation and computer technologies are understood, designed and exploited, joining elegant theory drawn from mathematics, engineering, psychology and design with the solving of practical problems
distinctiveFeatures: Computing studies how computation and computer technologies are understood, designed and exploited, joining elegant theory drawn from mathematics, engineering, psychology and design with the solving of practical problems
It underpins secure, reliable and usable systems of every size, is pervasive and often invisible and serves people's daily lives and careers
Its ways of working: disciplined problem-solving, design by choosing among alternatives with argued justification and control of complexity by abstraction and simplification and then integration
Innovation comes as much from foundational areas such as algorithmics and cryptography as from new technology

Seven discipline areas rest on computer science: computer science, computer engineering, software engineering, information technology, information systems, cybersecurity and data science; one degree may draw on several
Specialist degrees such as networking, games, multimedia, AI or health informatics count as computing when a discipline area informs their content; merely using computers in a field does not
The statement sets graduate outcomes, not a syllabus; the ACM and IEEE curricula give detailed content
Problem-solving and the making of artefacts are core, learned through practical, team and capstone work and through placements
Computing carries a particular responsibility to disabled people, since technology can remove barriers or raise them

computing's own responsibility to disabled people: universal access taught and practised, accessibility built into the software lifecycle and curricula designed for access beyond the statutory minimum (D1, 1.13; 1.14; 2.7 to 2.9)

subjectSpecific.text: You should be able to show how your computing knowledge is used by organisations, talking through examples and case studies.
Your course is meant to help you develop the ability to use what you know of computing, with computational thinking, to crack complex problems for the organisation you work in.
Your course is meant to help you develop the habit of planning and recording your own learning in core computing skills, as a basis for lifelong learning.
You should be able to use computer science, data science and digital technology to help solve problems in other subjects, working with people from those fields.

transferable.text: Your course is meant to help you develop acting with integrity in your professional conduct and behaviour.
Your course is meant to help you develop an awareness of the legal and ethical principles that govern computing work.
Your course is meant to help you develop an awareness of the sustainability issues computing raises.
Your course is meant to help you develop an understanding that computing is a global profession.
Your course is meant to help you develop the habit of using social media responsibly at work, including how you write online and by email and how you present yourself.
Your course is meant to help you develop critical reflection and clear communication in writing, in speech and online.
Your course is meant to help you develop a high standard of numeracy and literacy.
Your course is meant to help you develop the ability to deal with others professionally and with respect.
Your course is meant to help you develop respect for equality and diversity, understood and shown, across the many sectors where computing is practised.
Your course is meant to help you develop an understanding of what a leader does in setting direction and owning decisions.
Your course is meant to help you develop the confidence to speak up in meetings, in person or online.
Your course is meant to help you develop the ability to adapt quickly as situations and priorities change.
Your course is meant to help you develop the ability to make sense of data and information promptly, in study and at work.
Your course is meant to help you develop the ability to spot and use other people's skills and knowledge when you work together.
Your course is meant to help you develop the ability to pin down a problem and the outcome wanted and to negotiate a solution your colleagues accept.
Your course is meant to help you develop the ability to work without supervision, plan well and meet deadlines.
Your course is meant to help you develop the confidence to act on your own initiative.
Your course is meant to help you develop a professional network and the skills to grow it.
Your course is meant to help you develop a current, critical view of what is changing in the profession, at home and worldwide.
Your course is meant to help you develop the ability to make a short, reasoned case on a problem or opportunity to different audiences, in speech, online or in writing.
Your course is meant to help you develop an active habit of continuing professional development.
Your course is meant to help you develop an enterprising, questioning approach and a part in developing your profession.
Your course is meant to help you develop the ability to find relevant ideas and share them well in different formats with different audiences.
Your course is meant to help you develop the ability to see how environmental and social factors create openings or problems for computing systems.
You should get to know the many careers open to you in computing, what each asks for and what your own skills are, so you can match them to what you want to do.
You should be able to explain to an employer how your study and experience show your strengths and skills, including through a professional online profile.
Employers will expect you to be able to work with people from many cultures towards shared goals, as you do in group projects and presentations.
Employers will expect you to be able to take responsibility, stay flexible and resilient, get started without being asked, speak up when it is right to and plan and manage your time.
Employers will expect you to be able to look honestly at yourself and show awareness of different people and cultures, with emotional intelligence and empathy.
Employers will expect you to be able to listen well and produce clear, well-organised communications in different media.
Employers will expect you to be able to network with peers and watch for chances to push digital capability forward and improve the future.

statements.paraphrase: Because computing reaches everywhere, a curriculum can be authentic, tied to real problems and a force for social justice; it should matter to every student and be valued by them, and should give students culturally grounded practical work in a welcoming, collaborative setting, so that the technology they build carries no unintended bias.

forPractitioner.text: Build a curriculum every student can see themselves in: draw practical tasks from varied cultures, keep the setting welcoming and collaborative and teach students to check what they build for bias.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course team or institution; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.paraphrase: Curricula should therefore represent every student, recognising and removing the biases already present and supporting all students equally; the gender imbalance in computer science, partly the product of gendered terms, teaching habits and history, is the example given.

forPractitioner.text: Look through terminology, teaching approaches and examples for bias, gendered language included, remove what you find and support every student on equal terms.

statements.paraphrase: Computing courses should take up the sustainable development agenda by pointing to the economic, social and environmental issues the discipline affects for good or ill, and should help students build the personal and professional competencies to meet the challenges named in the UN Sustainable Development Goals in their later careers; the QAA and Advance HE ESD guidance sets out teaching approaches.

forPractitioner.text: Show students where computing helps or harms economically, socially and environmentally, and build the competencies they will need to act on the SDGs at work; use the ESD guidance for methods.

forPractitioner.text: Use the broad meaning of sustainability when planning the curriculum: alongside environmental topics such as data centre energy and e-waste, bring in social justice and economic prosperity.

statements.paraphrase: Computing has a particular responsibility to disabled people: technology can make once hard or impossible tasks routine, but it can also raise barriers, so care should be taken that it enables rather than disables.

forPractitioner.text: Teach universal access and practise it, with standards and assistive technologies; make accessibility a normal concern in the curriculum, for example wherever software lifecycles are taught.

statements.paraphrase: Curricula should be designed with accessibility in mind and meet statutory requirements at the least; putting access first lets students study who otherwise could not, and a requirement to attend campus regularly is an example of a barrier.

forPractitioner.text: Design the course with access as a primary concern, treating legal requirements as the floor; question anything, such as compulsory regular attendance, that shuts some students out.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course team or institution; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

forBeneficiary.text: Each year of your course builds towards the minimum subject and general skills you need at the end, and with a second-class result or better you can expect to be ready for postgraduate study.

forBeneficiary.text: If you study computing with another subject, you will gain part of the computing skills and add others from your second subject.

statements.paraphrase: Courses should also consider involving learners in monitoring and review as part of their partnership with students.

statements.paraphrase: Teachers should weigh subject-specific against transferable skills in curriculum and assessment, personalised learning and evidence of individual capability, as well as education against workforce needs; the value of learning should be clear, problem-solving and building artefacts are core, and capstone work and teamwork are encouraged.

forPractitioner.text: Balance subject and transferable skills, individual evidence and employer needs as you develop the course; make the value of learning clear and use capstone work and teamwork.

statements.appliesTo: teaching methods in computing courses
statements.paraphrase: Computing teaching is varied, which is a strength; the methods used should deliver learning shown through the learning outcomes, as evidence of capability, and should make sure learners gain competence in particular areas, which needs the ability to work independently in them.

forPractitioner.text: Choose teaching methods that let students show capability through the outcomes and also build competence, with independent work, in specific areas.

statements.appliesTo: teaching in computing courses
statements.paraphrase: Teaching should get students to reflect, evaluate, select, justify, communicate and innovate in solving problems, and prepare them to be adaptable, independent learners for life; students should meet a range of bespoke, open source and commercial tools; varied prior learning should be understood and accommodated, barriers minimised and EDI carefully considered.

forPractitioner.text: Teach so that students reflect, justify and innovate in problem-solving; use bespoke, open source and commercial tools; accommodate varied backgrounds and remove barriers to learning.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course team or institution; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.appliesTo: curriculum design
statements.paraphrase: Curriculum design should reflect research, scholarship and current industry practice and the ability to choose the right approach for a context; teaching sits within computing's legal, ethical, social, professional, economic and environmental setting; the curriculum should use inclusive design and cover sustainability and EDI, and graduates' attitudes and values should be developed for a diverse, fast-changing subject.

forPractitioner.text: Ground the curriculum in research and industry practice, set teaching in its legal, ethical and wider context, design it inclusively and cover sustainability and EDI.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course team or institution; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.appliesTo: undergraduate and master's computing courses
statements.about: from breadth to focus across levels
statements.paraphrase: Undergraduate courses typically start broad and narrow in the final year; generalist master's usually aim at the minimum subject knowledge of a computing graduate, broadly or in a niche, and specialist master's and integrated master's final years focus more closely; progression through levels should also move from general foundations towards current research and the state of the art, with growing independence in learning.

forPractitioner.text: Plan progression from broad foundations to focus, and from general knowledge towards current research, with students taking more charge of their own learning at each level.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course team or institution; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.appliesTo: computing curricula and students
statements.paraphrase: The curriculum will define what students learn and the outcomes show where graduates will have knowledge, competence or capability; each student is expected to have the chance to build deeper competence in some areas, through applied contexts, the capstone or optional modules, and may show it in a portfolio, through badges or in a CV.

forPractitioner.text: Use the curriculum and outcomes to define what all graduates know and can do, and give each student room to build deeper competence in chosen areas and to evidence it.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course sets out what you will learn, and you will also have the chance to build deeper competence in some areas you choose, which you can show in a portfolio, through badges or in your CV.

statements.appliesTo: institutions and staff delivering computing courses
statements.paraphrase: Hardware and software resources should support practical delivery; staff should show ongoing development in the subject and in pedagogy, supported by their institution, and would normally hold qualifications above the level they teach and a teaching qualification for higher education, held or in progress.

forPractitioner.text: Provide hardware and software for practical work, support staff development in computing and in teaching and expect staff to be qualified beyond the level they teach.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course team or institution; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.appliesTo: institutions offering integrated specialist master's courses
statements.paraphrase: An institution that offers an integrated specialist master's must be able to show why it is well placed to teach the topic, which often means staff at its forefront and engaged in advanced scholarship.

forPractitioner.text: If you offer an integrated specialist master's, be ready to justify your standing in the topic, usually through staff active at its forefront.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course team or institution; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.appliesTo: computing graduates at every award covered
statements.about: grounding knowledge and applying it to new technology
statements.paraphrase: Computing graduates need a firm grounding in core knowledge and the ability to apply it to keep learning and to become competent in new technologies as they appear; students would usually show they can learn and apply a new approach, often in the major activity near the end of the course.

forPractitioner.text: Secure a strong base of core knowledge and test students' ability to learn and apply something new, often in the final major activity.

forBeneficiary.text: You need a firm base of core computing knowledge and the ability to use it to learn new technologies as they appear, which you would usually show in your final major project.

statements.appliesTo: course delivery
statements.paraphrase: Course delivery should offer learning applied in real or simulated workplaces, such as placements or apprenticeships; sizeable team projects simulate real-world complexity, and projects set with industry or research partners can strengthen learning, self-regulation and awareness of legal and ethical issues.

forPractitioner.text: Build in placements or simulated work, sizeable team projects and projects set with industry or research partners.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course team or institution; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.appliesTo: assessment in computing courses
statements.paraphrase: Assessment in computing should be varied, fitting and engaging and, above all, authentic, tied to real contexts and constraints and letting students show their skills in practice.

forPractitioner.text: Design varied, engaging assessment that mirrors real contexts and lets students show their skills practically.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course team or institution; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.appliesTo: assessment design
statements.paraphrase: Academic integrity matters and assessment design is central to every student succeeding: assessment should let students show what they can do, not only write about it, with checkpoints so that only students' own work is assessed, for example by following QAA's contract cheating guidance.

forPractitioner.text: Design assessments where students show what they can do, with checkpoints that confirm the work is their own; use the contract cheating guidance.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course team or institution; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.appliesTo: capstone activities at master's level
statements.about: capstone formats; research literature at master's level
statements.paraphrase: A written dissertation may not suit every computing course, so a capstone may include academic papers, a professional portfolio or entrepreneurial work; at master's level such activities should focus more on research literature.

forPractitioner.text: Offer capstone formats beyond the dissertation where they fit; at master's level, make research literature central to them.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course team or institution; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.appliesTo: providers judging achievement
statements.about: evidence of achievement and Annex D
statements.paraphrase: Most students will perform well above the minimum threshold; each provider sets what counts as evidence of this and should refer to Annex D, which describes the four honours classes; the standards are expected to underpin awards, and any departure from them is to be identified and justified.

forPractitioner.text: Use Annex D's descriptions of the 1st, 2:1, 2:2 and 3rd as the common reference when deciding how to evidence achievement above threshold, and record and justify any departure from the standards.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course team or institution; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Undergraduate standards: threshold, typical and excellent descriptors

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in computing
statements.about: threshold in every category; rungs and classes
statements.paraphrase: Honours graduates in computing must show at least threshold attainment in every outcome category; threshold usually corresponds to a third, typical to a 2:1 or 2:2 and excellent to a first, and a first does not need excellence in every category.

forPractitioner.text: Make sure every honours graduate reaches at least the threshold in all six categories; use the typical and excellent rungs to describe second and first-class work.

forBeneficiary.text: To gain an honours degree in computing, you must reach at least the minimum level in every outcome area; a first does not mean being excellent in all of them.

headingPath: Undergraduate standards: threshold, typical and excellent descriptors

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in computing, at the threshold rung
statements.about: the main body of subject knowledge
statements.paraphrase: At threshold, honours graduates will show the understanding of the core body of computing knowledge that their subject needs.

forPractitioner.text: Every honours graduate must reach this in subject knowledge, understanding and skills: they show the understanding of the core body of computing knowledge that their subject needs. Teaching and assessment need to secure it for all.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum for an honours degree, you will show that you understand the core knowledge of your area of computing well enough for what it needs.

headingPath: Undergraduate standards: threshold, typical and excellent descriptors

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in computing, at the excellent rung
statements.about: the main body of subject knowledge
statements.paraphrase: At the excellent rung, honours graduates will show an exceptional grasp of the core body of knowledge with insightful critical judgement in using it, apply what the curriculum covers creatively and with innovation and reach past what was taught.

forPractitioner.text: First-class work in subject knowledge, understanding and skills usually shows this: graduates show an exceptional grasp of the core body of knowledge with insightful critical judgement in using it, apply what the curriculum covers creatively and with innovation and reach past what was taught. Leave room in tasks for the strongest students to show it.

forBeneficiary.text: At the excellent level, you will show an exceptional grasp of the core knowledge of your area, judge insightfully how to use it, apply it creatively and go beyond what you were taught.

headingPath: Undergraduate standards: threshold, typical and excellent descriptors

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in computing, at the typical rung
statements.about: the main body of subject knowledge
statements.paraphrase: At the typical rung, honours graduates will show a sound grasp of the core body of knowledge in their subject and use critical judgement in applying it.

forPractitioner.text: Most honours graduates reach this in subject knowledge, understanding and skills: they show a sound grasp of the core body of knowledge in their subject and use critical judgement in applying it. Design teaching and assessment so it is the usual result.

forBeneficiary.text: At the typical level, you will show a sound grasp of the core knowledge of your area and use critical judgement in applying it.

headingPath: Undergraduate standards: threshold, typical and excellent descriptors

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in computing, at the threshold rung
statements.paraphrase: At threshold, honours graduates will understand and use the subject's essential concepts, principles and practices in clearly defined scenarios, choosing and applying tools and techniques with judgement.

forPractitioner.text: Every honours graduate must reach this in intellectual skills: they understand and use the subject's essential concepts, principles and practices in clearly defined scenarios, choosing and applying tools and techniques with judgement. forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum for an honours degree, you will understand and use the essential ideas and methods of your subject on clearly set problems, choosing suitable tools with care.

headingPath: Undergraduate standards: threshold, typical and excellent descriptors

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in computing, at the excellent rung
statements.paraphrase: At the excellent rung, honours graduates will analyse critically and apply a wide range of the subject's ideas, principles and practices in open scenarios, choosing and using tools and techniques with refined judgement and adaptability.

forPractitioner.text: First-class work in intellectual skills usually shows this: graduates analyse critically and apply a wide range of the subject's ideas, principles and practices in open scenarios, choosing and using tools and techniques with refined judgement and adaptability. forBeneficiary.text: At the excellent level, you will analyse critically and apply a wide range of ideas and methods to open problems, choosing tools with refined judgement and adapting readily.

headingPath: Undergraduate standards: threshold, typical and excellent descriptors

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in computing, at the typical rung
statements.paraphrase: At the typical rung, honours graduates will analyse critically and apply the subject's ideas, principles and practices where scenarios are only loosely defined, choosing and using tools and techniques with effective judgement and adaptability.

forPractitioner.text: Most honours graduates reach this in intellectual skills: they analyse critically and apply the subject's ideas, principles and practices where scenarios are only loosely defined, choosing and using tools and techniques with effective judgement and adaptability. forBeneficiary.text: At the typical level, you will analyse critically and apply your subject's ideas and methods to loosely defined problems, choosing tools well and adapting as you go.

headingPath: Undergraduate standards: threshold, typical and excellent descriptors

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in computing, at the threshold rung
statements.paraphrase: At threshold, honours graduates will use judgement, critical thinking and problem-solving to solve clearly specified problems and build computational artefacts with some independence.

forPractitioner.text: Every honours graduate must reach this in computational problem-solving: they use judgement, critical thinking and problem-solving to solve clearly specified problems and build computational artefacts with some independence. Teaching and assessment need to secure it for all.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum for an honours degree, you will use judgement and critical thinking to solve clearly set problems and build working software or other artefacts with some independence.

headingPath: Undergraduate standards: threshold, typical and excellent descriptors

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in computing, at the excellent rung
statements.paraphrase: At the excellent rung, honours graduates will bring sophisticated judgement and critical thinking, research design and strong problem-solving to bear with considerable autonomy, building highly effective computational artefacts where circumstances are complex and unpredictable.

forPractitioner.text: First-class work in computational problem-solving usually shows this: graduates bring sophisticated judgement and critical thinking, research design and strong problem-solving to bear with considerable autonomy, building highly effective computational artefacts where circumstances are complex and unpredictable. forBeneficiary.text: At the excellent level, you will bring sophisticated judgement, research design and strong problem-solving to complex, unpredictable problems with real independence, building highly effective artefacts.

headingPath: Undergraduate standards: threshold, typical and excellent descriptors

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in computing, at the typical rung
statements.paraphrase: At the typical rung, honours graduates will use detailed judgement, critical thinking and problem-solving to solve both clearly specified and loosely defined problems and build suitable computational artefacts.

forPractitioner.text: Most honours graduates reach this in computational problem-solving: they use detailed judgement, critical thinking and problem-solving to solve both clearly specified and loosely defined problems and build suitable computational artefacts. forBeneficiary.text: At the typical level, you will use detailed judgement and critical thinking to solve both clearly set and loosely defined problems and build suitable artefacts.

headingPath: Undergraduate standards: threshold, typical and excellent descriptors

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in computing, at the threshold rung
statements.paraphrase: At threshold, honours graduates will identify and analyse a problem, then suitably design, build, test, integrate or deploy a computing system with its related artefacts, understanding how the stages connect.

forPractitioner.text: Every honours graduate must reach this in practical skills across the computing lifecycle: they identify and analyse a problem, then suitably design, build, test, integrate or deploy a computing system with its related artefacts, understanding how the stages connect. forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum for an honours degree, you will identify and analyse a problem and then design, build, test, integrate or deploy a system to solve it, knowing how the stages fit together.

headingPath: Undergraduate standards: threshold, typical and excellent descriptors

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in computing, at the excellent rung
statements.paraphrase: At the excellent rung, honours graduates will identify and analyse a problem, then suitably design, build, test, integrate or deploy a highly complex computing system with its related artefacts, understanding in depth how the stages connect and applying sophisticated problem-solving and evidence-informed evaluation.

forPractitioner.text: First-class work in practical skills across the computing lifecycle usually shows this: graduates identify and analyse a problem, then suitably design, build, test, integrate or deploy a highly complex computing system with its related artefacts, understanding in depth how the stages connect and applying sophisticated problem-solving and evidence-informed evaluation. Leave room in tasks for the strongest students to show it.

forBeneficiary.text: At the excellent level, you will do the same for a highly complex system, with a deep grasp of how the stages fit together and sophisticated, evidence-based evaluation.

headingPath: Undergraduate standards: threshold, typical and excellent descriptors

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in computing, at the typical rung
statements.paraphrase: At the typical rung, honours graduates will identify and analyse a problem, then suitably design, build, test, integrate or deploy a complex computing system with its related artefacts, understanding how the stages connect and applying problem-solving and evidence-informed evaluation.

forPractitioner.text: Most honours graduates reach this in practical skills across the computing lifecycle: they identify and analyse a problem, then suitably design, build, test, integrate or deploy a complex computing system with its related artefacts, understanding how the stages connect and applying problem-solving and evidence-informed evaluation. forBeneficiary.text: At the typical level, you will do the same for a complex system, knowing how the stages fit together and judging your work on evidence.

headingPath: Undergraduate standards: threshold, typical and excellent descriptors

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in computing, at the threshold rung
statements.paraphrase: At threshold, honours graduates will work effectively, including in a team, using tools and techniques suitably to communicate, organise tasks and plan projects with guidance.

forPractitioner.text: Every honours graduate must reach this in interpersonal and team working skills: they work effectively, including in a team, using tools and techniques suitably to communicate, organise tasks and plan projects with guidance. Teaching and assessment need to secure it for all.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum for an honours degree, you will work well, including in a team, using suitable tools to communicate, organise tasks and plan projects with some guidance.

headingPath: Undergraduate standards: threshold, typical and excellent descriptors

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in computing, at the excellent rung
statements.paraphrase: At the excellent rung, honours graduates will work in a highly proactive, accomplished way, including leading within a team, using tools and techniques excellently to communicate, organise tasks and plan projects proficiently with little guidance.

forPractitioner.text: First-class work in interpersonal and team working skills usually shows this: graduates work in a highly proactive, accomplished way, including leading within a team, using tools and techniques excellently to communicate, organise tasks and plan projects proficiently with little guidance. Leave room in tasks for the strongest students to show it.

forBeneficiary.text: At the excellent level, you will work in a highly proactive, accomplished way, taking a lead in your team and using tools excellently to plan and run projects with little guidance.

headingPath: Undergraduate standards: threshold, typical and excellent descriptors

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in computing, at the typical rung
statements.paraphrase: At the typical rung, honours graduates will work proactively and effectively, including in a team, using tools and techniques well to communicate clearly, organise tasks and plan projects with little guidance.

forPractitioner.text: Most honours graduates reach this in interpersonal and team working skills: they work proactively and effectively, including in a team, using tools and techniques well to communicate clearly, organise tasks and plan projects with little guidance. Design teaching and assessment so it is the usual result.

forBeneficiary.text: At the typical level, you will work proactively and well in a team, using tools to communicate, organise tasks and plan projects with little guidance.

headingPath: Undergraduate standards: threshold, typical and excellent descriptors

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in computing, at the threshold rung
statements.paraphrase: At threshold, honours graduates will identify suitable practices and carry out their own work inside a professional, legal and ethical framework that covers data management and use, security, EDI and sustainability.

forPractitioner.text: Every honours graduate must reach this in professional practice: they identify suitable practices and carry out their own work inside a professional, legal and ethical framework that covers data management and use, security, EDI and sustainability. Teaching and assessment need to secure it for all.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum for an honours degree, you will choose suitable practices and work within professional, legal and ethical limits, including on data, security, equality and sustainability.

headingPath: Undergraduate standards: threshold, typical and excellent descriptors

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in computing, at the excellent rung
statements.paraphrase: At the excellent rung, honours graduates will identify the best practices of their kind and reach highly principled solutions inside a professional, legal and ethical framework that deal consistently with a wide range of relevant considerations, such as data management and use, security, EDI and sustainability, in their own work.

forPractitioner.text: First-class work in professional practice usually shows this: graduates identify the best practices of their kind and reach highly principled solutions inside a professional, legal and ethical framework that deal consistently with a wide range of relevant considerations, such as data management and use, security, EDI and sustainability, in their own work. Leave room in tasks for the strongest students to show it.

forBeneficiary.text: At the excellent level, you will choose the best practices available and reach highly principled solutions that deal consistently with a wide range of professional, legal and ethical issues in your work.

headingPath: Undergraduate standards: threshold, typical and excellent descriptors

statements.appliesTo: honours graduates in computing, at the typical rung
statements.paraphrase: At the typical rung, honours graduates will identify suitable practices and reach principled solutions inside a professional, legal and ethical framework that deal with the core considerations, such as data management and use, security, EDI and sustainability, in their own work.

forPractitioner.text: Most honours graduates reach this in professional practice: they identify suitable practices and reach principled solutions inside a professional, legal and ethical framework that deal with the core considerations, such as data management and use, security, EDI and sustainability, in their own work. forBeneficiary.text: At the typical level, you will choose suitable practices and reach principled solutions that deal with the main professional, legal and ethical issues in your work, from data and security to equality and sustainability.

statements.appliesTo: all master's graduates in computing
statements.paraphrase: Every master's graduate has deep, advanced knowledge and understanding of their subject or profession, shaped by practice, scholarship and research; this will include critical awareness of current issues and developments, critical skills, an understanding of professional ethics, integrity and responsibility and the capacity to reflect on how they are progressing as learners.

forPractitioner.text: Make sure master's graduates leave with advanced, current knowledge, critical skills, a grasp of professional ethics and the habit of reflecting on their own learning.

forBeneficiary.text: At master's level, you will have advanced, up-to-date knowledge of your subject or profession, critical skills, an understanding of professional responsibility and ethics and the habit of reflecting on how you are progressing.

statements.appliesTo: graduates of research, specialist and professional master's
statements.about: what each kind of master's graduate can do
statements.paraphrase: Research master's graduates are likely also to study independently and use advanced research methods; specialist or advanced study master's graduates are likely to complete a research project, sometimes with a critical literature review; and professional or practice master's graduates are able to bring research and critical perspectives to professional situations and use methods suited to their practice.

forPractitioner.text: Match outcomes to the kind of master's: independent study and research methods for research master's, a research project for specialist ones and research applied to practice for professional ones.

forBeneficiary.text: Depending on your master's, you are likely to study independently with advanced research methods, complete a research project, or, on a professional master's, bring research and critical thinking to real work situations.

statements.appliesTo: postgraduate computing courses
statements.about: postgraduate content aligned to level 7 or 11
statements.paraphrase: In every case, a postgraduate course's content should align with the specification for FHEQ level 7 or SCQF level 11.

forPractitioner.text: Check that the content of each postgraduate course matches the FHEQ level 7 (SCQF level 11) descriptor.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course team or institution; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.appliesTo: postgraduate master's graduates in computing
statements.paraphrase: With reference to the undergraduate descriptors, postgraduate computing graduates must show at least threshold attainment in every relevant outcome category; threshold usually corresponds to a Pass.

forPractitioner.text: Make sure every master's graduate reaches at least the threshold in each category that applies to the course; a Pass usually marks it.

forBeneficiary.text: To gain a postgraduate degree in computing, you must reach at least the minimum level in every outcome area that applies to your course, which usually means a Pass.

statements.appliesTo: postgraduate master's graduates in computing, at the excellent rung
statements.paraphrase: At the excellent rung, master's graduates will show deep, systematic understanding of knowledge in their area, much of it at or shaped by the forefront, with critical awareness and advanced understanding of current problems or recent developments, originality in applying knowledge and a practical and reflective grasp of how research and enquiry techniques, both established and state-of-the-art, create and interpret knowledge.

forPractitioner.text: Distinction-level work in subject knowledge, understanding and skills usually shows this: graduates show deep, systematic understanding of knowledge in their area, much of it at or shaped by the forefront, with critical awareness and advanced understanding of current problems or recent developments, originality in applying knowledge and a practical and reflective grasp of how research and enquiry techniques, both established and state-of-the-art, create and interpret knowledge.

forBeneficiary.text: At the excellent level on a master's, you will show a deep, systematic understanding of your area, much of it close to the leading edge, an advanced and critical view of its current problems, originality in using what you know and a reflective grasp of how established and the newest research methods build knowledge.

statements.appliesTo: postgraduate master's graduates in computing, at the typical rung
statements.paraphrase: At the typical rung, master's graduates will show systematic understanding of knowledge in their area of study, much of it at or shaped by the forefront of the discipline or of professional practice, critical awareness of current problems or recent developments, some originality in applying knowledge and a practical understanding of how established research and enquiry techniques create and interpret knowledge.

forPractitioner.text: Most master's graduates reach this in subject knowledge, understanding and skills: they show systematic understanding of knowledge in their area of study, much of it at or shaped by the forefront of the discipline or of professional practice, critical awareness of current problems or recent developments, some originality in applying knowledge and a practical understanding of how established research and enquiry techniques create and interpret knowledge.

forBeneficiary.text: At the typical level on a master's, you will show a systematic understanding of your area, much of it close to the leading edge, a critical awareness of its current problems, some originality in using what you know and a practical grasp of how research builds knowledge.

statements.appliesTo: postgraduate master's graduates in computing, at the excellent rung

statements.appliesTo: postgraduate master's graduates in computing, at the typical rung

forBeneficiary.text: At the typical level on a master's, you will analyse, apply and critically judge the ideas and practices at the leading edge of your area.

statements.appliesTo: postgraduate master's graduates in computing, at the excellent rung
statements.paraphrase: At the excellent rung, master's graduates will show innovation or originality with sophisticated judgement, critical thinking, research design and strong problem-solving, working with considerable autonomy to build comprehensive, highly effective computational artefacts under complex or open constraints.

forPractitioner.text: Distinction-level work in computational problem-solving usually shows this: graduates show innovation or originality with sophisticated judgement, critical thinking, research design and strong problem-solving, working with considerable autonomy to build comprehensive, highly effective computational artefacts under complex or open constraints.

forBeneficiary.text: At the excellent level on a master's, you will bring innovation or originality and sophisticated judgement to problems you tackle largely on your own, building comprehensive, highly effective artefacts under complex or open constraints.

statements.appliesTo: postgraduate master's graduates in computing, at the typical rung

forBeneficiary.text: At the typical level on a master's, you will use judgement, critical thinking and research design to solve problems largely on your own, building effective artefacts when the constraints are complex or open.

statements.appliesTo: postgraduate master's graduates in computing, at the excellent rung
statements.about: applying computing techniques in complex scenarios

statements.appliesTo: postgraduate master's graduates in computing, at the typical rung
statements.about: applying computing techniques in complex scenarios
statements.paraphrase: At the typical rung, master's graduates will apply computing techniques suited to their area systematically in complex or unpredictable scenarios, making sound decisions when data are incomplete or missing.

forPractitioner.text: Most master's graduates reach this in practical computing skills: they apply computing techniques suited to their area systematically in complex or unpredictable scenarios, making sound decisions when data are incomplete or missing.

forBeneficiary.text: At the typical level on a master's, you will apply suitable computing techniques systematically in complex, unpredictable situations and make sound decisions when data are missing.

statements.appliesTo: postgraduate master's graduates in computing, at the excellent rung
statements.paraphrase: At the excellent rung, master's graduates will show self-direction in tackling and solving complex problems and approach and carry out tasks in a highly proactive, effective way.
